name: Rhode Island T. F. Green International Airport
before:
Rhode Island's main airport, at Warwick 6 miles south of Providence, and the largest of the six airports run by the Rhode Island Airport Corporation. Around 7.5 million people live within roughly 90 minutes of it.

The train connection is what makes it useful beyond Rhode Island. The airport sits directly beside the Northeast Corridor and has its own station, T. F. Green Airport, on the MBTA Providence/Stoughton line, reached by an elevated walkway from the terminal. The station opened in November 2011 and has carried services to Providence and Boston, so a client can arrive here and continue by rail rather than road.

There are two concourses, North with 14 gates and South with eight. Gates 7 and 8 handle international arrivals and connect directly down to customs on the lower level.

It opened in 1931 and was the first state-owned airport in the United States. It is named after Theodore Francis Green, a Rhode Island governor and long-serving senator, and the terminal, rebuilt in 1996, is named after another governor, Bruce Sundlun.
after:
Rhode Island's main airport, at Warwick 6 miles south of Providence. It is the largest of the six airports run by the Rhode Island Airport Corporation.

The train connection is what makes it useful beyond Rhode Island. It has its own station, TF Green Airport, on the MBTA Providence/Stoughton line, reached by an elevated walkway from the terminal. Commuter trains run from there to Providence and Boston on weekdays only, so a client arriving Monday to Friday can continue by rail rather than road.

The terminal has two concourses, North and South. International arrivals clear customs on the lower level.

It opened in 1931 and was the first state-owned airport in the United States. The name honours Theodore Francis Green, a Rhode Island governor and long-serving senator, and the terminal, rebuilt in 1996, is named after another governor, Bruce Sundlun.

claims.claim: 7.5 million people within roughly 90 minutes
claims.wasBefore: Around 7.5 million people live within roughly 90 minutes of it.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. Not on the operator's About PVD page, media guide, strategic business plan or master plan page (three tries).

claims.claim: sits directly beside the Northeast Corridor
claims.wasBefore: The airport sits directly beside the Northeast Corridor
claims.why: No second source names the corridor. The Providence Journal (15 January 2022) says Amtrak trains 'now pass through' the airport's Interlink station, and Wikipedia says Amtrak does not stop there, so the corridor is no use to a client at the airport; the trains that stop are the MBTA's, which the text keeps.

claims.claim: station opened in November 2011
claims.why: Probably wrong, and not worth replacing. Wikipedia contradicts itself (constructed October 2010, 'opened in November 2011', and 'Upon opening in December 2010, the station saw limited service'); the operator's own timeline says 'The InterLink Transportation Hub opens, along with a rental car facility and MBTA commuter rail service' under 2010. No second non-Wikipedia source for the 2010 date was found, and the date does not matter to a booking.

claims.claim: North with 14 gates and South with eight
claims.wasBefore: North with 14 gates and South with eight
claims.why: Sources disagree. Wikipedia gives 14 and eight (22); the operator's live terminal map lists 20 gate numbers (1 to 12, 14 to 19, 21 and 22) under a 'Gates(18)' heading. The two concourses themselves are kept.

claims.claim: gates 7 and 8 are the international arrival gates
claims.wasBefore: Gates 7 and 8 handle international arrivals and connect directly down to customs
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. The operator's pages put gates 7 and 8 in the South Concourse ('South Concourse by gates 7 & 8') and describe customs on the first level, but never say which gates take international arrivals. Softened to the customs point.
